newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Vranitzky wins Albania deal amid fresh violence.
newsitem.headline: Vranitzky wins Albania deal amid fresh violence.

text.p: European security envoy Franz Vranitzky on Thursday said he has won a new deal on elections to stop Albania sliding back into chaos as more violence struck in the south of the country.
Vranitzky was to stay in Albania to make sure the deal stuck after an agreement last week unravelled almost as soon as he left the country.

The elections are seen as a key element to prevent more unrest in Albania, which exploded into an orgy of violence in February and March after hundreds of thousands of people lost money in collapsed high-risk pyramid investment schemes.

Vranitzky said he persuaded politicians to amend an electoral law that had caused most political parties to threaten to boycott the vote as they said it favoured the former ruling party of President Sali Berisha.
The deal was won as more violence struck in the south of the troubled nation when an ammunition dump exploded.

Three men were missing and were presumed dead after the blast, which caused a huge crater at the dump in the region of the southernmost town of Gjirokaster, according to an Italian spokesman for the multinational force in Albania.
He also said four were injured although initial reports said that 14 were wounded.
The blast left a huge crater and a pall of smoke as it ripped apart surface depots at the dump near the town of Picar, some 18 km (10 miles) north of Gjirokaster.
Vranitzky clearly warned the Albanian politicians that they were under close international scrutiny over the compromise.

"I very clearly said to political leaders...that further delays as far as a compromise on the elections is concerned will not improve the situation and will put into question the international community's willingness to provide economic and financial support," he told a news conference.
Vranitzky said he persuaded political parties to pass a new electoral law after most political parties threatened to boycott the planned elections.
The parties said a law forced through parliament by the Democratic Party of President Sali Berisha favoured Berisha.

Vranitzky said the electoral law would be brought back to parliament on Thursday evening. He also said that an election law prepared by an interim Government of National Reconciliation would also be discussed.

He said that if the compromise was not respected the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), the Council of Europe and other international bodies would reconsider their commitment to monitor the elections, vital for them to be considered as free and fair.
At parliament, a long statement was handed out with the details of how the law should be amended, setting out the division of proportional representation and majority voting.
The split between the two systems had also been a cause of concern for the parties, which favoured more seats to be decided on a proportional basis while the Democrats backed more majority voting.
The Socialists pulled out of the last elections in May 1996, which international observers said were flawed.
To meet a target date of June 29 for the election, Berisha would, by law, have to issue a decree on Thursday, 45 days before the vote.
